standard.title: Democracy, elections and representatives
standard.description: the key values and features of Australia's democracy, including elections, and the roles and responsibilities of elected representatives
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS4K07 (Rules and laws) and AC9HS4K08 (Local government and services): Students explain why rules and laws exist and how local government provides services to communities.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the key values and features of Australia's democracy, including the electoral system, and describe the roles and responsibilities of elected representatives at different levels.

nodes.label: What is democracy?
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the meaning of democracy and identify the key values underpinning Australian democracy, including freedom of election, assembly, speech and religion, the rule of law, and human rights.
nodes.minimum_width: Define democracy and name two key values of Australian democracy.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the meaning of democracy and describe the range of key values: freedom of election and being elected, freedom of assembly and political participation, freedom of speech and religious belief, rule of law, and basic human rights. Illustrate how these values apply in familiar contexts.
wider: Compare Australian democratic values with those of a non-democratic system of government to highlight what distinguishes democracy
Explore the Australian citizenship pledge and the federal government's statement of Australian values, evaluating what these documents reveal about the ideals of Australian democracy
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't understand the core values of democracy will treat elections as a procedural mechanism without understanding what they protect or enable. The values framework is the conceptual foundation for understanding why elections, representatives and citizenship responsibilities exist.

response_modes.reason: Use concrete, familiar examples (class vote, school council, local election) to illustrate each value. Abstract democratic values become accessible when applied to contexts students already understand.

success_criteria: Students explain what democracy means and name at least three key values of Australian democracy.
Students give an example of how at least one democratic value applies in a context they are familiar with.

nodes.label: Features of Australia's electoral system
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the key features of Australia's electoral system, including the secret ballot, compulsory voting, preferential voting, and the role of the Australian Electoral Commission.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe two features of Australia's electoral system and explain the purpose of each.
nodes.typical_width: Explain all key features of Australia's electoral system: the secret ballot, compulsory voting, preferential voting system, and the role of the Australian Electoral Commission in administering free and fair elections.
wider: Investigate how Australia's voting system has changed over time, including when women and First Nations Australians were first allowed to vote, and evaluate what these changes reveal about democracy as an evolving system
Compare Australia's electoral system with that of another country, identifying similarities and differences in features such as voting age, compulsory voting and vote-counting methods

response_modes.reason: The historical expansion of voting rights (women, First Nations Australians) adds essential context to understanding electoral features as choices made and contested, not natural givens.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The history of voting rights expansion in Australia — particularly for First Nations Australians and women — is a rich and important direction that connects electoral features to broader civic and historical understanding.
success_criteria: Students describe at least two features of Australia's electoral system and explain the purpose of each.
Students explain the role of the Australian Electoral Commission.

nodes.label: Roles and responsibilities of elected representatives
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the roles and responsibilities of elected representatives, including making laws, representing constituents and being accountable to voters.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe two responsibilities of an elected representative at one level of government.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the roles and responsibilities of elected representatives at different levels (local, state/territory, federal), including making and debating laws, representing the views of their constituents, and being accountable through elections.
wider: Investigate the work of a specific elected representative (e.g. a local councillor or federal MP) over a period of time, and evaluate how effectively they have represented their community
Explore what characteristics make for a 'good' representative at different levels of government, and consider whether current representatives meet these criteria

response_modes.reason: The distinction between levels of government (local, state, federal) is important groundwork for Year 6 content — ensure students can differentiate roles and responsibilities across levels, not just describe them in the abstract.

success_criteria: Students describe at least two roles or responsibilities of elected representatives.
Students give an example of how a representative is accountable to voters.

nodes.label: Responsibilities of citizens in a democracy
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the responsibilities of citizens in a democracy, including enrolling to vote, being informed, voting responsibly, and participating in civic life.
nodes.minimum_width: Name two responsibilities of citizens in a democracy and explain why each matters.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the responsibilities of citizens in a democracy: enrolling to vote, being informed about candidates and issues, voting responsibly, and participating in civic life through community groups, advocacy or other means.
wider: Investigate how citizens participate in democracy beyond voting, including through petitions, public submissions, community groups and protest, and evaluate the effectiveness of different forms of participation
Examine examples of citizens working together to achieve a democratic goal (connecting to AC9HS5K07) and assess the role of shared values in making collective civic action effective

response_modes.reason: This node connects the features and values of democracy to what they require of citizens. Use a structured reflection on how democratic values (Node 1) are enacted through specific citizen responsibilities — make the conceptual link explicit.

success_criteria: Students explain at least two responsibilities of citizens in a democracy.
Students connect at least one citizen responsibility to a democratic value (e.g. being informed connects to freedom of election).
Students use correct civic terms (e.g. 'elector', 'representative', 'electoral roll').
